questions.question: Define a longitudinal profile, distinguish a graded from an ungraded profile, and explain the difference between permanent and temporary base levels.
questions.expected_answer: A longitudinal profile is a side view of a river along its full length from source to mouth. A graded profile is a smooth, concave curve — steep at the source, flattening to the mouth — with erosion and deposition in balance and no interruptions; an ungraded profile is irregular, broken by waterfalls over resistant rock, rapids, and level stretches ponded behind reservoirs. Base level is the lowest level to which the river can erode: the permanent base level is sea level, which the river can never cut below, while temporary base levels — a reservoir or a resistant rock band — only locally and temporarily halt downward erosion until the river removes or bypasses them.

questions.question: Explain why the two banks of a meander bend have different shapes, naming each bank and the process responsible.
questions.expected_answer: Water crosses a bend at two speeds: on the outside it travels the longer path fastest, and this energetic water erodes, undercutting and collapsing the bank, producing the steep undercut slope or river cliff. On the inside the water travels the short path slowly, cannot carry its load, and deposits sand and gravel, building the gentle slip-off slope or point bar. Fast outer water erodes while slow inner water deposits, so the bend deepens on the outside and shallows on the inside, and with each flood the loop enlarges and migrates across the valley floor.

questions.question: Give the eight-step sequence by which a meander becomes an oxbow lake and finally a meander scar.
questions.expected_answer: Sustained erosion attacks the outer banks of both limbs of the loop; deposition builds the inner banks; the neck of land between the limbs is narrowed from both sides; a major flood breaks through the thinned neck; the shorter, steeper breach becomes the main channel; sediment deposited at the loop's two junctions seals it off; the severed loop remains as a horseshoe-shaped oxbow lake; cut off from flow, the lake evaporates, silts up with overbank floods and is invaded by reeds until only a curved marshy meander scar remains — as seen across the Pongola floodplain in northern KwaZulu-Natal.
